title: Getting around
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: This module speaks the polite third person throughout, because a stranger in the street is the scene. Giri, Prenda and Vada join M1's Scusi and Senta, and they are the same kind of thing: present SUBJUNCTIVE forms arriving as frozen politeness words, with L3 to show the paradigm. Their tu partners — gira, prendi, va' — exist and are not written here.

TRANSPORT TAKES IN: vado in autobus, in treno, in macchina, in metropolitana. Not con and not per. English "by bus" and Spanish "en autobús" both mislead a little, and walking breaks the pattern anyway — a piedi, with a and not in, for no reason a rule can give. Learn the list.

a destra and a sinistra are taught WHOLE, as one thing each. That keeps the bare a where L1 put it and gives the direction its own note — there is nothing to build here, and a learner who tries to assemble it from a plus a noun will get the article wrong.

Come si va a…? uses the impersonal si — "how does one go". It is the same si hiding inside L1-M1's si chiama, which was taught as a whole phrase precisely so the bare word would still be free when a module needed it. It makes a sentence with no subject at all.

l'autobus is ONE index key and does not answer for autobus. The elision keeps the apostrophe inside the token, so the engine sees a different word — which is why both are taught here, and why in autobus (no article) and l'autobus (with one) have to be met separately.

sentences.cue: Excuse me, where is the square?

words.note: The double z is held and said ts: pee-AT-tsa. In an Italian town it is the reference point everything else is given from.
The general word. via is what appears on a sign with a name after it, and the two are not swapped.

sentences.trap: dov'è asks about a place both of you know exists. To ask whether there is one at all, Italian uses c'è — C'è una piazza qui? — which is L1-M7's row doing a different job.
sentences.sound: do-VE la pee-AT-tsa. dov'è is one word with the stress at the end.

variations.cue: Excuse me, where is the station?
Excuse me, where is the road?
Excuse me, where is the bridge?

mistake.why: The elision is compulsory here: Scusi, dov'è la piazza?

sentences.usage: Stopping someone in the street — M1's opener doing its job.
sentences.mnemonic: dov'è for a place you both know is there.

words.note: Another frozen subjunctive, beside M1's Scusi and Senta. The tu form is gira, and it is not written in this course.
One thing, not two. There is no article inside it and none can be added — a la destra is not Italian.
Singular in Italian where English says "the lights". The stress is on the second syllable — se-MA-fo-ro.
Masculine, and an -e noun, so its plural is in -i. It also means a long weekend, which is a joke about bridging two holidays.

sentences.trap: a destra has no article and takes none. English's "to the right" and Spanish's a la derecha both put one in, and both mislead.
sentences.sound: JEE-ree a DE-stra. The gi is soft, and the whole imperative is two light syllables.

variations.display: Giri a destra dopo il ponte

mistake.display: Giri a la destra al semaforo
mistake.why: The phrase takes no article: Giri a destra al semaforo.

sentences.usage: Giving directions to someone who has stopped you.
sentences.mnemonic: a destra, a sinistra — no article, ever.

words.note: The polite imperative of andare, and it looks nothing like vado or va. Irregular verbs are where the frozen-form policy earns its keep.
In directions it means "keep going" rather than "always". Sempre dritto is one of the most-heard phrases in an Italian street.
Both spellings are current and mean the same thing here. diritto also means "a right" as in a legal one, which dritto does not.
a destra's pair, and built the same way — one whole thing with no article inside it.

sentences.trap: sempre is not doing its dictionary job. Vada sempre dritto is "keep straight on", not "always go straight", and the word is nearly compulsory in the phrase.
sentences.sound: VA-da SEM-pre DREET-to. Three words, three stresses on the first syllable, which is what makes it easy to shout across a street.

variations.display: Vada sempre dritto e giri a sinistra
variations.cue: Keep straight on and turn left
variations.changed: a second instruction joined with e
without sempre — shorter, and less usual

mistake.why: The polite form is vada: Vada sempre dritto.

sentences.usage: The first half of nearly every set of directions.
sentences.mnemonic: sempre dritto — keep going, not always.

sentences.display: Prenda la prima strada a destra
sentences.cue: Take the first street on the right
sentences.literal: Take the first street to right

words.note: The polite imperative of prendere, L1-M6's verb. It takes a street, a bus, a coffee — the same range English gives "take".
Ordering things here — la prima strada. The same word means "before" as an adverb, which is the opposite of dopo.
Invariable. On its own at a door it means "come in", which is the answer to M1's Permesso.

sentences.trap: prima agrees like an ordinary adjective — la prima strada, il primo ponte — because that is what it is. It only stops agreeing when it means "before".
sentences.sound: PREN-da la PREE-ma STRA-da. The r of prenda is tapped once, never rolled.

variations.display: Prenda la prima strada a sinistra
variations.cue: Take the first street on the left

variations.changed: a vehicle rather than a street

variations.display: Vada avanti e prenda la prima strada
variations.cue: Go on and take the first street

mistake.display: Prenda il primo strada a destra
mistake.why: strada is feminine: Prenda la prima strada a destra.

sentences.usage: The precise half of a set of directions.

sentences.cue: The bar is round the corner

words.note: Invariable, and it does both place and time — dopo l'angolo, dopo le sette. Its opposite as an adverb is prima.
The article elides into the noun and the whole thing is ONE index key. The bare angolo is here in the forms so both shapes are taught together.

sentences.trap: l'angolo is a single word to the engine and to the ear. That is the same policy L1 set with l'acqua and l'italiano — an elision fuses, and the fused shape has to be learnt as its own word.
sentences.sound: DO-po LAN-go-lo. The article and noun run together with no break at all.

variations.display: Il bar è dopo il ponte
variations.cue: The bar is after the bridge
variations.changed: a landmark that takes no elision

variations.cue: The cinema is round the corner
The stop is round the corner

mistake.display: Il bar è dopo il angolo
mistake.why: A vowel takes the elided article: dopo l'angolo.

sentences.usage: Answering someone who asked where something is.
sentences.mnemonic: An elision fuses, and the fusion is a word.

sentences.cue: I take the bus every day

words.note: One key, like l'angolo. It does NOT answer for a bare autobus — the engine sees two different words, and both have to be taught.
Invariable in the plural — gli autobus — because it ends in a consonant. In autobus, with no article at all, is how you say "by bus".
A bus or tram stop. A railway station is a stazione and never a fermata, though a small one may be called both.

sentences.trap: Three shapes of the same idea sit in this module: l'autobus with the article, autobus bare after in, and gli autobus in the plural. None of them is derived from the others.
sentences.sound: LAOO-to-boos. The stress is on the first syllable, which is where Italian differs from English's "bus".

variations.cue: I take the bus at seven

variations.changed: no article at all, which is what in requires

mistake.why: in takes no article here: Vado in autobus.

sentences.usage: Saying how you get about, which comes up early with anyone new.

sentences.display: Vado a piedi, non in macchina
sentences.literal: I-go on feet, not in car

words.note: The one member of the transport set that takes a rather than in, and there is no reason behind it. One whole thing, and the bare piedi is not what a learner needs.
Literally a machine, and it is the ordinary word for a car. The cch is a long hard k.
Shortened to metro in speech, and both are used. Feminine, because the long form is an adjective agreeing with a noun nobody says any more.

sentences.trap: Every other means of transport takes in and this one takes a. It is not a pattern with an exception — it is a list, and a piedi is on it.
sentences.sound: a pee-E-dee. Three syllables, and the two vowels of piedi are both sounded.

variations.display: Vado in treno, non in macchina
variations.cue: I'm going by train, not by car

mistake.display: Vado in piedi, non in macchina
mistake.why: Walking takes a: Vado a piedi, non in macchina.

sentences.usage: Arranging how to get somewhere, or correcting an assumption about it.
sentences.mnemonic: Everything takes in. Feet take a.

words.note: As an adverb here it does not move — è lontano whatever the subject. As an adjective in front of a noun it agrees normally.
The bare adverb, beside L1-M7's vicino a, which needs the a to name what it is near. Without the a it simply means "close by".

sentences.trap: L1-M7 taught vicino a — near something. This is the same word standing alone, and dropping the a changes it from a preposition into an adverb.
sentences.sound: lon-TA-no. The o's are pure and short, and the stress is on the middle syllable.

variations.changed: a masculine subject — and lontano does not move

mistake.why: As an adverb it does not agree: La stazione è lontano?

sentences.usage: The follow-up to every set of directions, and it decides whether you walk.
sentences.mnemonic: vicino a points at something. vicino alone does not.

sentences.display: Scusi, come si va a Roma?
sentences.cue: Excuse me, how do you get to Rome?
sentences.literal: Excuse-yourself, how one goes to Rome?

words.note: The impersonal si — "how does one go". It is the same si inside L1-M1's si chiama, which was taught whole precisely so the bare word stayed free for this.

sentences.trap: There is no subject and none is missing. si va is a complete verb phrase meaning "one goes", and English's nearest match is the vague "you" that means anybody.
sentences.sound: KO-me see VA. si is short and unstressed, leaning onto the verb after it.

variations.cue: How do you get to Milan?
How do you get to the station?
variations.changed: in rather than a, which places take

variations.display: Scusi, come si va a Milano?
variations.cue: Excuse me, how do you get to Milan?

mistake.display: Scusi, come lei va a Roma?
mistake.why: The impersonal has no subject: Scusi, come si va a Roma?

sentences.usage: Asking the way when you do not know what the route even is.
sentences.mnemonic: si va — one goes, and nobody is named.

words.note: The gli is the soft ly of M2's figlio. It covers a train ticket, a cinema ticket and a banknote alike.
What English calls a platform, Italian names by the track number: binario tre. Its plural drops one i — binari — as vecchio did.

sentences.trap: A ticket window takes no verb at all. Un biglietto, per favore is a complete transaction, and adding vorrei only makes it politer, never more correct.
sentences.sound: bee-LYET-to. The gli is one soft sound and the double t is held.

variations.changed: the next question after the ticket
a verdict rather than a request

mistake.why: One ticket is singular: Un biglietto, per favore.

sentences.usage: At a station window or a machine — and the platform question follows immediately.
sentences.mnemonic: Italy counts platforms by the track.
